titre: Do Grains and Legumes Really Need to Be Eaten Together?
accroche: In the 1970s, a bestseller insisted on combining grains and legumes in the same meal. Its author retracted the claim ten years later.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1971, a young American woman worried about the ecological cost of livestock farming publishes a book that will become a worldwide bestseller, *Diet for a Small Planet*, selling more than three million copies. Frances Moore Lappé explains how to eat without meat, and devotes a large part of the book to one precise rule: plant proteins, called “incomplete” because they lack one or more essential amino acids in sufficient quantity, must be combined in the same meal with another source that fills the gap, grains with legumes, grains with dairy, seeds with legumes, or the body supposedly couldn't use them properly. The book gives tables of exact proportions to follow.

## A Real Scientific Idea, Misapplied to the Meal

The underlying idea isn't invented: the biological value of a protein mixture, meaning the share of the amino acids it supplies that the body can actually use, is an old and solid notion in nutrition science. What doesn't hold up is the same-meal requirement. The body keeps a pool of free amino acids in the blood and liver, replenished by digestion from previous hours, which it draws on as needed: it doesn't need the two halves of a complete protein to arrive together on the same plate. In 1981, in the tenth-anniversary edition of her book, Lappé herself acknowledges the problem, on page 162: she had given the impression that getting enough protein without meat required far more care than it actually does, and removes from later editions the proportion tables she had published ten years earlier.

## The Shift

The science that followed confirms the retraction rather than the original claim: a 1994 review in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition concludes that a variety of plant proteins covers amino acid needs without any need to pair them in the same meal, and the American Dietetic Association says so in 2009 in its official position on vegetarian diets. Yet the advice to combine grains and legumes never really disappeared from cookbooks or family conversations. Following it isn't harmful, a bowl of rice and lentils remains a good meal, but a rule invented to solve a problem that didn't exist at that scale kept circulating long after its own author abandoned it. A false idea, carried by a book that sells, spreads at exactly the same speed as a true one.

repere.texte: In the tenth-anniversary edition of *Diet for a Small Planet* (1981, p. 162), Frances Moore Lappé acknowledges having given the impression that getting enough protein without meat required far more care than it actually does, and removes the proportion tables she had published in 1971.

carte.punch: Grains and legumes in the same meal: a rule its own author abandoned.
carte.idee: In 1971, Diet for a Small Planet insisted on combining certain plant proteins in the same meal. In 1981, its author, Frances Moore Lappé, admitted she had been wrong: the body combines amino acids over the course of a whole day, not just within a single plate.

quiz.question: Why isn't it necessary to eat grains and legumes in the same meal to get enough protein?
choix: Because the body keeps a reserve of free amino acids and can combine whatever was eaten over the course of the day
Because legumes actually contain all the essential amino acids in sufficient amounts on their own
Because the human body doesn't build proteins from plant-derived amino acids
Because the idea of protein complementation was invented with no scientific basis at all
quiz.explication: The body keeps a reserve of amino acids that it combines over several hours, not only within the same meal. Legumes remain low in certain amino acids, the body does build proteins from plant sources, and the complementation idea was based on a real scientific notion, the biological value of proteins, misapplied to the timing of meals.
